content.intro: This lesson covers Platform Licensing and Operational Responsibilities. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Professional Docker work is version-aware and documented: distinguish image production from orchestration, check supported platform and license terms, preserve reproducible build/runtime configuration, and record the evidence needed for handoff, upgrade, recovery, and review. Learning platform licensing and operational responsibilities helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Supported deployment environments
items.text: A container port and a published host port are different values. Bind publishing deliberately, especially when a service should be reachable only from the local machine.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
